query: generative AI doctoral students writing efficiency

llm_major: The only conflict lists 10.1007/s44217-025-00602-7 (a Grammarly writing experiment with EFL postgraduates) on side A, but side A's statement about accelerated progress, research quality and supervisory relationships comes only from 10.14742/ajet.8843, so the pairing mixes two different outcomes and tools.

rq5 covers skill erosion, integrity violations and bias, yet the table has no graduate-level evidence on them: the support is perception surveys (10.1007/s10639-024-13151-7, 10.1186/s41239-023-00411-8), commentaries (10.53761/1.20.02.07, 10.1080/07294360.2023.2280200), and a truncated general-student study (10.1186/s41239-024-00444-7).
llm_minor: The consensus claim that structured, feedback-oriented AI use improves writing pools a doctoral n=10 correlational study, a Grammarly experiment and 10.3390/educsci15020141 (Chinese-as-a-second-language learners), which do not cover the same population, tool or outcome.

The first consensus claim cites 10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1259531 (intention to use) and 10.1111/ijal.12574 (language learning) as support for reported efficiency gains, but neither reports efficiency or productivity; only 10.14742/ajet.8843 and 10.1080/14703297.2023.2271445 do.

The conditional claims overstate moderators: 'gains appear only with iterative use' rests on n=10; the supervisor claim presents the authors' suggestion of a shifting role (10.14742/ajet.8843, plus the reli-2 10.14742/ajet.8598) as a dependency; and the discipline and appraisal findings come from undergraduate or general students.

rq4 lists AI literacy, English proficiency, supervisor guidance and discipline as moderators, but the table has no graduate-level study testing English proficiency, supervisor guidance or discipline effects; the evidence is undergraduate, general-student or qualitative.

The measurement half of rq6 (how productivity and quality of AI-assisted research are measured) has no direct source; 10.2196/53164 and 10.2196/56537 are truncated and cover one narrow topic, while the policy evidence is coursework-focused or conceptual.

No evidence in the table links task stages such as data analysis, coding or literature review to outcomes in graduate students: 10.3390/computers14020053 is a general higher-education review with a truncated abstract, and the literature-review studies are truncated, so rq3 is largely answered at the writing stage only.
actions: synthesize: restrict side A to 10.14742/ajet.8843 and, if the Grammarly study is kept, report it separately as measured writing gains with a non-generative feedback tool; also state that the contrast is perceived research progress versus perceived writing challenges, not a like-for-like conflict.

search rq5: empirical studies of over-reliance, deskilling, hallucinated citations, AI-detection or integrity incidents, and bias among master's/doctoral students or early-career researchers, preferably longitudinal, experimental or audit designs.

rationale: Only rq5 is flagged for search because the critic found it lacking graduate-level empirical evidence on over-reliance, deskilling, hallucinated citations, integrity incidents and bias. The new queries target experimental, audit and incident-based designs and use different vocabulary from the earlier perception-survey queries. Other critic issues concern synthesis or are not flagged for search, so no queries are added for them.

llm_major: rq3 passes on count, but the only graduate-level link between usage pattern and outcome is 10.1080/03075079.2024.2323593 (n=10, one writing task). Literature review, coding and analysis are covered only by non-graduate or truncated papers (10.3390/computers14020053, 10.2196/56537, 10.2196/53164), and the doctoral intention study 10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1259531 reports no outcomes.
llm_minor: The rq1 consensus is built only on 10.14742/ajet.8843 and 10.1080/14703297.2023.2271445. It omits 10.1007/s42438-023-00440-6 (UK academics), which questions whether generative AI relieves workload, and 10.1186/s41239-024-00444-7 (workload drives use), and it does not say how these cut against the claim of faster progress.

No paper in the table describes how productivity or quality of AI-assisted graduate research is measured. The measurement half of rq6 is unanswered, and only the policy half is covered, mostly by coursework or publisher documents.

The tentative claim that interactive or feedback-oriented AI use is linked to better writing leans on 10.3390/educsci15020141. That paper reports knowledge acquisition and motivation rather than better writing, and it concerns language learners. 10.1007/s44217-025-00602-7 is a non-generative tool.

The moderator gap says critical appraisal lowering perceived output quality (10.1186/s40561-025-00384-3) is in tension with 'framing critical interaction as beneficial'. No cited paper establishes that framing, and 10.1080/03075079.2024.2323593 concerns interactivity, not critical appraisal. Appraisal and interaction are being conflated.

rationale: Only rq3 was flagged for searching. The new queries target master's and doctoral samples, specific research tasks (literature screening, coding, data analysis), and usage-log or outcome measures, which the earlier general usage-pattern queries did not reach. The other critic issues concern synthesis or gap wording and need no new searches.

llm_major: No consensus or conditional claim addresses whether GenAI changes the quality of graduate research outputs, and rq2 rests on perceived quality (10.14742/ajet.8843), n=10 (10.1080/03075079.2024.2323593), and EFL/language-learner or undergraduate studies (10.1007/s44217-025-00602-7, 10.3390/educsci15020141), so the sub-question is effectively unanswered despite passing the count.

The measurement half of rq6 is effectively unanswered: no paper in the table describes how productivity or quality of AI-assisted graduate research is measured, and policy evidence covers coursework, publishers or general university frameworks (10.1057/s41599-024-03526-z, 10.12688/f1000research.142411.2, 10.1186/s41239-023-00408-3) rather than graduate research or theses.
llm_minor: Moderators named in rq4 (AI literacy, English proficiency, discipline, supervisor guidance) are mostly covered by undergraduate or general-student papers (10.1080/14703297.2025.2600476, 10.1186/s40561-025-00384-3) or a programming sample (10.1007/s10639-025-13337-7), and the discipline moderator is only inferred from an undergraduate STEM vs non-STEM comparison.

The second conflict pairs a single qualitative study of experienced research users (10.14742/ajet.8843) against a single small English-major study (10.54855/ijaile.25212), so the conflict is thin, and the 'postgraduates show greater awareness than undergraduates' claim in the second consensus rests on one single-university perception study (10.1016/j.heliyon.2024.e26239).

The literature-screening and coding gap cites 10.2196/47049, 10.2196/53164, 10.2196/56537 and 10.3390/computers14020053, all of which are truncated or non-graduate, so it does not demonstrate that graduate-user evidence is truly absent, and the design does not address how task stage affects outcomes.

search rq6: graduate or thesis-specific AI policies, doctoral supervision guidelines, and studies or reviews proposing or validating measures and rubrics of research productivity and quality for AI-assisted research
